hints: Think about which two subshells electrons can be removed from in a transition metal atom or ion.
walkthrough:
Compare the energies of the outer subshells**
Picture the electron arrangement of a first row transition metal, for example $\text{Fe}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{6}4s^{2}$. The $4s$ and $3d$ levels overlap in energy and are almost the same. That means removing a $4s$ electron costs about the same energy as removing a $3d$ electron, so different numbers of electrons can be removed without a large jump in energy.
Final answer: The $4s$ and $3d$ subshells are very close in energy, so electrons from both subshells can be lost to give different stable oxidation states.

hints: Recall the general shape of all d orbitals except $d_{z^2}$, and think about where the $d_{xy}$ lobes lie relative to the x and y axes.
walkthrough:
Place the four lobes correctly**
All d orbitals except $d_{z^2}$ look like a four leaf clover. For $3d_{xy}$, the whole shape lies flat in the xy plane. Draw four touching lobes meeting at the origin, rotated so the x and y axes pass through the gaps between lobes, not through the lobes themselves. The z axis should pass through the centre perpendicular to the lobes.
Final answer: Four lobes of equal size lying in the xy plane, centred on the origin, with each lobe pointing between the x and y axes.

hints: Start from the isolated ion where the five d orbitals have the same energy, then think what ligands do to that degeneracy.
Think about what happens when an electron moves between the two split sets of d orbitals and where the energy for that jump comes from.
Link the wavelength of light absorbed to the colour you actually see, remembering that the observed colour is what is left over.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals with ligands**
On its own, a $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion has five $3d$ orbitals all at the same energy. When ligands such as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ approach to form a complex, they repel d electrons unequally. Some d orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised in energy, others point between ligands and stay lower. So you get two sets with a gap, $\Delta E$.

Absorb light to promote an electron**
If the ion has a partly filled d subshell, an electron can jump from the lower set to the higher set. That jump needs exactly $\Delta E$. The electron takes this energy by absorbing one photon of visible light of matching frequency, where $\Delta E = hv$.

See the colour that is left behind**
White light minus the colour absorbed is what reaches your eye. So if red light is absorbed to drive the d to d transition, the complex looks blue-green. That is why we say the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour. A $d^{0}$ or $d^{10}$ ion cannot do a d to d transition and so is colourless or white.

Final answer: In the presence of ligands the five d orbitals are split into two sets of different energy.
When a d electron is promoted from the lower set to the higher set, energy equal to $\Delta E$ is absorbed from visible light.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to that absorbed.

hints: Recall the classic test for $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ with $\text{NaOH}$ and then with excess $\text{NH}_3$, and how the blue changes in depth.
walkthrough:
Remember the two familiar blues**
You are meeting two very famous copper blues here. Adding hydroxide gives solid $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$, a pale or light blue precipitate. Replacing water ligands by ammonia to give $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ changes the splitting energy and gives an intense dark or deep blue solution. Keep the pair in order: hydroxide is pale, ammine is deep.

Final answer: colour of $\text{Cu(OH)}_2(\text{s})$: pale / light blue precipitate
colour of $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}(\text{aq})$: dark / deep blue solution

hints: Identify which ion in equilibrium 3 is increased when $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ is added, and predict which way the system must shift to use it up.
walkthrough:
Apply Le Chatelier to equilibrium 3**
Look at equilibrium 3: $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu(OH)}_2(\text{s}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$. Adding $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ raises $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ on the left. The system opposes the change by using up added $\text{OH}^{-}$, so it moves to the right. That produces more solid $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$, which you see as a pale blue precipitate.
Final answer: Addition of $\text{NaOH}$ increases $[\text{OH}^{-}]$, so equilibrium 3 shifts to the right to decrease $[\text{OH}^{-}]$, forming $\text{Cu(OH)}_2(\text{s})$ precipitate.

hints: Think of the octahedral $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ as having six positions, and focus only on where the two identical $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands can sit relative to each other.

Sketch one isomer with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other at 180 degrees, and the other with them next to each other at 90 degrees, using solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines for 3D depth.
walkthrough:
Draw the trans form**
Put $\text{Cu}$ in the centre of an octahedron. For trans-$[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$, place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other, for example one up and one down along the vertical axis, at $180^{\circ}$. Fill the four equatorial positions with $\text{NH}_3$. Use a solid wedge for a bond coming out, a hashed wedge for a bond going back, and straight lines for bonds in the plane, so the octahedral 3D shape is clear.

Draw the cis form**
Now place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands side by side at $90^{\circ}$, for example one up and one to the right. Fill the other four octahedral positions with $\text{NH}_3$. This is cis-$[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$. Check you have six ligands in total in each diagram: $4 \times \text{NH}_3 + 2 \times \text{H}_2\text{O}$, with correct labels and 3D bonds.

Final answer: Trans isomer: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other (e.g. axial positions) with four $\text{NH}_3$ in the equatorial plane.
Cis isomer: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands adjacent at $90^{\circ}$ to each other, with four $\text{NH}_3$ occupying the remaining positions. Both drawn with correct 3D wedge/dash octahedral geometry.
